name: Anekathangapatham, Gaurikund
deity: Shiva as Anekathangapatheswarar, with the Goddess Gowri
period: A Himalayan Paadal Petra Sthalam of Vada Nadu, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century); identified by tradition with Gaurikund on the Kedarnath route
dynasty: Himalayan pilgrim halt on the Kedarnath route; no Tevaram-age structure is recorded
summary: Anekathangapatham, a northern shrine of the Tevaram sung by Sambandar, is identified by tradition with Gaurikund, where the Goddess is said to have done penance on the road to Kedarnath.

sections.history: Anekathangapatham is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of the five in Vada Nadu, the northern country of the Tevaram. Thirugnana Sambandar sang its Lord, and tradition holds that he did so from Srikalahasti, as he sang the other shrines of the far north. The Tevaram knows two places of this name: the other, Kachchi Anekathangapatham at Kanchipuram, was sung by Sundarar. The northern one is identified by tradition with Gaurikund in Rudraprayag district, the last road-head below Kedarnath, at about 1,980 metres in the valley of the Mandakini.
sections.architecture: Gaurikund is a small pilgrim settlement on the Kedarnath path rather than a temple town, and no Tevaram-age structure survives here. Its shrine to Gauri, the Goddess as the ascetic bride of Shiva, stands beside the place of the hot spring that gave the village its name; the great floods of 2013 swept much of the old kund away, though warm water still flows at the spot. The Mandakini runs below.
sections.legends: Local tradition holds that Parvati performed her long penance here to win Shiva as her husband, and that their marriage was celebrated at nearby Triyuginarayan. The Tevaram name is often read as the place of the elephant, anekatham being an old Tamil word for the elephant, and Gaurikund's own tradition links the Goddess with the birth of the elephant-headed Ganesha, whom she set to guard her as she bathed.
sections.festivals: The shrine follows the Kedarnath season: the valley fills with pilgrims from the opening of the Kedarnath temple in spring until it closes for winter. Maha Shivaratri and the Sambandar guru puja are times to recall the Tevaram shrine in Tamil temples; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: For most pilgrims, Gaurikund is the threshold of the climb to Kedarnath, where they bathe, worship the Goddess and set out on foot. A Tamil Shaiva pilgrim pauses here also for Sambandar's sake, honouring Anekathangapatham before walking up the valley to Kedarnath, another northern shrine of the Tevaram.

visit.timings: The Gauri shrine is open during the Kedarnath pilgrimage season, roughly from late April or May to October or November, from morning until evening. Confirm current timings and the season locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest dress is expected at the shrines; warm, layered clothing and sturdy walking shoes are essential in the mountains. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed outdoors along the pilgrim route; ask before photographing inside shrines or during worship.
visit.gettingThere: Vehicles stop at Sonprayag, a few kilometres below, from where shuttles run to Gaurikund; the trek to Kedarnath starts here. Rishikesh and Haridwar are the nearest major railheads, and Dehradun's Jolly Grant airport is the nearest airport, followed by a long road journey via Rudraprayag.
